prompt: The export has twelve orders, and `=COUNT(E2:E13)` answers 8. What does that tell you?
hint: What does COUNT count?

choices.text: Four rows of the Qty column are empty
choices.why: An empty cell would show as empty. These four show a quantity, with un after it.

choices.text: Four quantities are stored as text
choices.why: Right: the four typed with un. SUM skips them as well, which is why it answers 48.

choices.text: The column holds eight different quantities
choices.why: COUNT does not look for distinct values; it counts cells that hold numbers.

choices.text: Four of the twelve orders were cancelled in the old system
choices.why: Nothing in the export says so. The count is about the type of each value, not about the orders.

prompt: Before any cleaning, what does `=SUM(E2:E13)` answer on the `Old export` sheet?
hint: Only the cells that hold numbers are added.

prompt: `=COUNTIFS(F2:F13, "Wholesale")` answers 7, and eight orders are wholesale. Which row does it miss, and why?
hint: Conditions ignore one difference and not another.

choices.text: The row that says wholesale in lower case, because conditions match capitals exactly
choices.why: Conditions ignore case, so wholesale passes. The one that fails has something you cannot see.

choices.text: The row with WHOLESALE and a space after it
choices.why: Right. The space makes it a different word, and nothing on the screen shows it.

choices.text: Row 1, because COUNTIFS treats the header as data
choices.why: The range starts at F2; the header is not in it.

choices.text: The last row, because COUNTIFS stops one row early
choices.why: COUNTIFS reads every row of the range you give it.

prompt: Why does the lesson put every fix in a new column instead of correcting the cells where they are?
hint: Two reasons: what you can compare, and what happens next month.

choices.text: Excel refuses to edit cells that were pasted from another program
choices.why: Pasted cells are ordinary cells; you can type over them.

choices.text: A formula in the same cell would refer to itself, a circular reference
choices.why: That is true of a formula in the cell it reads, but nobody proposed that; the lesson's point is different.

choices.text: The original stays beside the fix, and next month reuses it
choices.why: Right: the formula works again on the next export. Each row can be compared with its source, and next month's file needs no retyping.

choices.text: New columns calculate faster than edited ones
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: What does `=LEN(C3)` answer on the `Old export` sheet, where C3 shows `  café aroma`?
hint: Spaces are characters.

prompt: What does `TRIM` return for `Padaria  Central`, which has two spaces between the words?
hint: TRIM does more than cut the ends.

choices.text: Padaria Central, with one space
choices.why: Right. Runs of spaces between words become one, and the ends lose theirs.

choices.text: Padaria  Central, unchanged, since TRIM only cuts the ends
choices.why: TRIM also turns every run of spaces between words into a single one.

choices.text: PadariaCentral, with every space removed
choices.why: That would be SUBSTITUTE replacing spaces with nothing. TRIM keeps one between words.

choices.text: PADARIA CENTRAL, in capitals
choices.why: TRIM never changes letters; UPPER does that.

prompt: After `TRIM`, `MATCH` finds `café aroma` in a customer list that spells it `Café Aroma`. Why does it match?
hint: What does every lookup ignore?

choices.text: TRIM also capitalises the first letter of each word
choices.why: TRIM only touches spaces. The text is still café aroma in lower case.

choices.text: MATCH ignores accents as well as case
choices.why: It ignores case only; CAFE DO LARGO fails for exactly that reason.

choices.text: Lookups ignore case
choices.why: Right. Only the spaces were in the way, and TRIM removed them.

choices.text: A MATCH with 0 accepts the nearest spelling
choices.why: 0 asks for an exact match, which is why the accent breaks it.

prompt: Row 7, `CAFE DO LARGO`, gives `#N/A` against the customer list, which says `Café do Largo`. What is the sound fix?
hint: Which difference is left once the spaces and the capitals are out of the way?

choices.text: Wrap the lookup in IFERROR so the row shows blank
choices.why: That hides the one row that needs a decision, and its order disappears from every count by customer.

choices.text: Use PROPER(TRIM(C7)) before the lookup
choices.why: Capitals are not the difference; lookups ignore them already. The É is.

choices.text: Replace every E with É across the column
choices.why: That would break every name with a plain E in it, which is most of them.

choices.text: Decide once, in writing, that this spelling is C04, or fix the old system
choices.why: Right. A letter and its accented form are different characters, and no formula knows which one a person meant.

prompt: `=PROPER(TRIM(C9))` turns `café do largo ` into `Café Do Largo`. What does the lesson conclude?
hint: What does PROPER do to every word?

choices.text: PROPER suits codes and channels, and not names with rules of their own
choices.why: Right. It capitalises every word, and the customer is called Café do Largo.

choices.text: PROPER is broken on accented letters and should never be used
choices.why: It handled the é correctly. The trouble is the word do, which it capitalised as it always does.

choices.text: TRIM should come after PROPER, not before
choices.why: The order of the two makes no difference to the capital D.

choices.text: The customer list is wrong and should say Café Do Largo
choices.why: The list holds the name as the customer writes it; the function does not know Portuguese.

prompt: A space at the end of a word is invisible on screen. To see it, count the characters in the cell with the function ___.
hint: Its name is short for length.

prompt: What does `=FIND(" - ", D2)` answer, where D2 holds `SUL1K - Sul de Minas 1 kg`?
hint: Count the characters from 1 up to the space before the hyphen.

prompt: `=LEFT(D2, 5)` gives `SUL1K` on row 2. Why does the lesson not fill that down the column?
hint: Look at row 3.

choices.text: LEFT cannot be filled down
choices.why: It fills like any formula. The problem is the fixed 5.

choices.text: Some codes have six characters, so a fixed 5 cuts DEC250 to DEC25
choices.why: Right. FIND measures each row's own separator, so one formula serves both lengths.

choices.text: LEFT returns a number, and the codes must be text
choices.why: LEFT always returns text.

choices.text: D2 holds a formula, and LEFT reads only typed values
choices.why: D2 holds pasted text, and LEFT would read a formula's result anyway.

prompt: The old system sends this export every month. Why does the lesson prefer the `FIND` formula to Flash Fill?
hint: What is left in the cells after each one?

choices.text: Flash Fill exists only in Microsoft 365 and not in older Excel
choices.why: Flash Fill has been in Excel for many versions; the reason is what it leaves behind.

choices.text: Only the formula carries over to next month's rows
choices.why: Right: Flash Fill leaves values that must be redone and rechecked. For a list that comes back, the work should be written down once.

choices.text: Flash Fill cannot read text that has spaces inside it
choices.why: It reads them; the trouble is that it guesses a pattern and stores the result as values.

choices.text: Formulas always calculate faster than Flash Fill
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

prompt: Put in order what `=UPPER(LEFT(D2, FIND(" - ", D2)-1))` does to `cer1k - Cerrado 1 kg`, innermost first.
hint: Excel works from the inside of the formula out.
items: Subtract one: the code is 5 characters
Take 5 characters from the left: cer1k
trap: Taking characters before knowing how many is the fixed-length mistake the formula exists to avoid.

prompt: Why does `=VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(E2, " un", ""))` work on both `6 un` and the plain number 12?
hint: What does SUBSTITUTE return when it finds nothing to replace?

choices.text: SUBSTITUTE skips cells that hold numbers
choices.why: It does not skip them: it reads 12 as the text 12 and returns it unchanged.

choices.text: VALUE ignores any letters it finds in the text
choices.why: VALUE fails on letters, which is why the un has to be removed first.

choices.text: SUBSTITUTE hands 12 back as text, and VALUE converts both
choices.why: Right: on 12 there is nothing to replace, so one formula fills the whole column.

choices.text: Excel converts the whole column to numbers once one cell is fixed
choices.why: Every cell is converted by its own formula; nothing spreads.

prompt: With column L filled, what does `=SUM(L2:L13)` answer?
hint: Every quantity is a number now.

prompt: Order `00841` shows as `841` after the paste. Which statement about it is right?
hint: Why can TEXT repair this column, and when could it not?

choices.text: The zeros are still in the cell, and a number format will show them again
choices.why: The value stored is 841; a format can draw zeros, but the text 00841 is gone.

choices.text: TEXT(A2, "00000") gives it back, only because all orders have five digits
choices.why: Right. With codes of varying length nothing left in the cell says how many zeros there were.

choices.text: VALUE(A2) restores it, since VALUE reads the original text
choices.why: VALUE makes numbers, and 841 already is one.

choices.text: Nothing went wrong: 841 and 00841 are the same order
choices.why: To whoever searches the old system they are different identifiers.

prompt: Which of these columns should be stored as text, even when every value is made of digits? Choose all that apply.
hint: Will it ever be added up?

choices.text: A postcode
choices.why: It is matched and read, never added, and some start with zero.

choices.text: A phone number
choices.why: An identifier, not a quantity; the sum of two phone numbers means nothing.

choices.text: The number of bags in a sale
choices.why: A quantity: it is added, averaged and compared, so it must be a number.

choices.text: An order number such as 00841
choices.why: An identifier with leading zeros, which a number cannot keep.

choices.text: The price paid per bag
choices.why: A quantity, multiplied by the bags to give revenue.

prompt: B2 of `Old export` holds `20241202`. What does `=DATE(LEFT(B2,4), MID(B2,5,2), RIGHT(B2,2))` give?
hint: DATE(year, month, day).

choices.text: The text 2024-12-02
choices.why: DATE returns a day number, not text; the format decides how it is drawn.

choices.text: 20241202 unchanged, because LEFT returns text
choices.why: DATE converts its text arguments into numbers on its own.

choices.text: 12 February 2024
choices.why: MID(B2,5,2) is the month, 12, and RIGHT(B2,2) the day, 02.

choices.text: 45628, shown as 2 December 2024
choices.why: Right: a real date, which a date condition and every date function can use.

prompt: On the `Sales` sheet, how many days does `=B109-B2` answer?
hint: Dates are numbers, so this is a subtraction.

prompt: A workbook made in São Paulo has `=DATEVALUE(P6)` with P6 holding the text `03/12/2024`. It is opened in New York, in an Excel set to US English. What does the cell show?
hint: Who decides the order of day and month for DATEVALUE?

choices.text: 3 December 2024, because the workbook remembers where it was made
choices.why: DATEVALUE reads the text by the regional setting of the computer it runs on.

choices.text: #VALUE!, because the text is in the Brazilian order
choices.why: 03 and 12 are both valid months, so nothing fails.

choices.text: 12 March 2024, with no error
choices.why: Right. Two computers, two answers, and neither warns. DATE with RIGHT, MID and LEFT says the order in the formula.

choices.text: The text unchanged, since DATEVALUE only converts ISO dates
choices.why: It converts any text the regional setting can read as a date.

prompt: On the `Sales` sheet, B2 holds 2 January 2025. Match each formula to what it returns.
hint: One function per piece, and EOMONTH for the end.

prompt: A pasted date column has some values against the right edge of their cells and some against the left. What happened?
hint: Lesson 1: what does alignment say about a value?

choices.text: The cells have two different alignment formats
choices.why: Alignment here is Excel's default, which follows the type of the value.

choices.text: Day-first dates were read month first
choices.why: Right: days up to 12 became wrong dates and the rest stayed text, and the wrong dates look exactly like right ones.

choices.text: Half the dates carry a time of day and half do not
choices.why: A time would still be a number, on the right.

choices.text: The column is wider than the dates
choices.why: Width does not change which side a value sits on.

prompt: With the cleaned columns J and L in place, how many bags did the wholesale orders of the export hold?
hint: One SUMIFS over the cleaned columns, never the original ones.

prompt: Next month's export has a quantity written `7 bags`. What does the column L formula answer on that row?
hint: The formula removes one exact piece of text.

choices.text: 7, because VALUE ignores the word after the number
choices.why: VALUE cannot read letters; only un was removed, and bags is still there.

choices.text: #VALUE!, and that is what you want: the row does not fit the pattern
choices.why: Right. A formula that guessed would hide the row; the error makes somebody look at it.

choices.text: 0, since SUBSTITUTE finds nothing to replace
choices.why: SUBSTITUTE returns the text unchanged, and VALUE then fails on it.

choices.text: The text 7 bags, unchanged
choices.why: VALUE is the last step, and it either returns a number or an error.
